claim: Filamentous fungal and oomycete plant pathogens that invade by direct penetration through the leaf epidermal cell wall cause devastating plant diseases.
source: Filamentous fungal and oomycete plant pathogens that invade by direct penetration through the leaf epidermal cell wall cause devastating plant diseases.
evidence: This is a general statement about plant pathogens that draws from established scientific knowledge in plant pathology.

claim: Plant preinvasive immunity toward nonadapted filamentous pathogens is highly effective and durable.
source: Plant preinvasive immunity toward nonadapted filamentous pathogens is highly effective and durable.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific consensus in plant immunity research.

claim: Pre- and postinvasive immunity correlates with the formation of evolutionarily conserved and cell-autonomous cell wall structures, named papillae and encasements, respectively.
source: Pre- and postinvasive immunity correlates with the formation of evolutionarily conserved and cell-autonomous cell wall structures, named papillae and encasements, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and established knowledge in the field.

claim: It is still unresolved how papillae/encasements are formed and whether these defense structures prevent pathogen ingress.
source: Yet, it is still unresolved how papillae/encasements are formed and whether these defense structures prevent pathogen ingress.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current scientific knowledge.

claim: In Arabidopsis, the two closely related members of the SYP12 clade of syntaxins (PEN1 and SYP122) are indispensable for the formation of papillae and encasements.
source: Here, we show that in Arabidopsis the two closely related members of the SYP12 clade of syntaxins (PEN1 and SYP122) are indispensable for the formation of papillae and encasements.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Loss-of-function mutants of PEN1 and SYP122 were hampered in preinvasive immunity toward a range of phylogenetically distant nonadapted filamentous pathogens.
source: Moreover, loss-of-function mutants were hampered in preinvasive immunity toward a range of phylogenetically distant nonadapted filamentous pathogens, underlining the versatility and efficacy of this defense.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased penetration frequencies in mutant plants.

claim: SYP12s from the early diverging land plant, Marchantia polymorpha, can complement the function of Arabidopsis SYP12s.
source: Complementation studies using SYP12s from the early diverging land plant, Marchantia polymorpha, showed that the SYP12 clade immunity function has survived 470 million years of independent evolution.
evidence: This is supported by experimental complementation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The SYP12 clade immunity function has survived 470 million years of independent evolution.
source: Complementation studies using SYP12s from the early diverging land plant, Marchantia polymorpha, showed that the SYP12 clade immunity function has survived 470 million years of independent evolution.
evidence: This is inferred from the complementation data and knowledge of evolutionary timescales.

claim: Ancestral land plants evolved the SYP12 clade to provide a broad and durable preinvasive immunity to facilitate their life on land.
source: These results suggest that ancestral land plants evolved the SYP12 clade to provide a broad and durable preinvasive immunity to facilitate their life on land and pave the way to a better understanding of how adapted pathogens overcome this ubiquitous plant defense strategy.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings regarding evolutionary function.

claim: Plants assemble localized preinvasive papillae and postinvasive encasements at sites of attempted cell entry in response to attack by filamentous pathogens.
source: In response to attack by filamentous pathogens, plants assemble localized preinvasive papillae and postinvasive encasements at sites of attempted cell entry (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B; Hückelhoven and Panstruga, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and visual evidence in the figure.

claim: Papillae and encasements are thought to contain antimicrobial cargo that provide effective and durable immunity against diverse filamentous pathogens.
source: These conserved defense structures are thought to contain antimicrobial cargo that provide effective and durable immunity against diverse filamentous pathogens, and fossil evidence suggests that these structures appeared very early in the evolution of land plants (O'Connell and Panstruga, 2006; Krings et al., 2007; Overdijk et al., 2016; Hansen and Nielsen, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and represents current scientific understanding.

claim: Fossil evidence suggests that papillae and encasements appeared very early in the evolution of land plants.
source: These conserved defense structures are thought to contain antimicrobial cargo that provide effective and durable immunity against diverse filamentous pathogens, and fossil evidence suggests that these structures appeared very early in the evolution of land plants (O'Connell and Panstruga, 2006; Krings et al., 2007; Overdijk et al., 2016; Hansen and Nielsen, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to paleobotanical research.

claim: Direct evidence that papillae/encasements contribute to immunity against nonadapted pathogens is still lacking.
source: However, although their frequent association with resistance to nonadapted pathogens is well-known, direct evidence that papillae/encasements contribute to immunity against these pathogens is still lacking.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the current scientific literature.

claim: The secretory syntaxin PEN1 is required for the timely formation of papillae to hamper penetration by nonadapted powdery mildew fungi.
source: The discovery that the secretory syntaxin PEN1 is required for the timely formation of papillae to hamper penetration by nonadapted powdery mildew fungi highlighted the key role played by membrane trafficking in plant immunity (Collins et al., 2003; Nielsen et al., 2012; Nielsen and Thordal-Christensen, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PEN1 (also referred to as syntaxin of plants 121 or SYP121) is a Qa-SNARE primarily located at the plasma membrane.
source: PEN1 (also referred to as syntaxin of plants 121 or SYP121) is a Qa-SNARE primarily located at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the protein's classification and localization.

claim: The ARF-GEF, GNOM, regulates recycling of PEN1 between the plasma membrane and the trans-Golgi network.
source: On the other hand, the ARF-GEF, GNOM, regulates recycling of PEN1 between the plasma membrane and the trans-Golgi network, where it is needed for a fast papilla response (Nielsen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: PEN1 is thought to mediate membrane fusion both at the plasma membrane and at the trans-Golgi network.
source: Accordingly, PEN1 is thought to mediate membrane fusion both at the plasma membrane and at the trans-Golgi network.
evidence: This is an inference based on the protein's function and localization.

claim: The ROR2 syntaxin in barley is orthologous to PEN1.
source: The ROR2 syntaxin in barley is orthologous to PEN1 (Collins et al., 2003), suggesting that the preinvasive immunity dependent on PEN1 or ROR2 was present in early angiosperms before the divergence of monocots and dicots, spanning some 140 million years (My) of evolution.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The preinvasive immunity dependent on PEN1 or ROR2 was present in early angiosperms before the divergence of monocots and dicots, spanning some 140 million years of evolution.
source: The ROR2 syntaxin in barley is orthologous to PEN1 (Collins et al., 2003), suggesting that the preinvasive immunity dependent on PEN1 or ROR2 was present in early angiosperms before the divergence of monocots and dicots, spanning some 140 million years (My) of evolution.
evidence: This is an inference based on orthology and evolutionary timescales.

claim: Focal accumulation of GFP-PEN1 at attack sites in response to Blumeria graminis f.sp. hordei (Bgh) is also seen for ROR2 in barley.
source: Focal accumulation of GFP-PEN1 at attack sites in response to Blumeria graminis f.sp. hordei (Bgh) is also seen for ROR2 in barley and highlights a likely conserved functionality in plant defense against powdery mildews (Bhat et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The strong extracellular accumulation of GFP-PEN1 signal localized to fungal attack sites can be explained by the secretion of extracellular vesicles, also known as exosomes.
source: The strong extracellular accumulation of GFP-PEN1 signal localized to fungal attack sites can be explained by the secretion of extracellular vesicles, also known as exosomes, which accumulate to a high degree in both papillae and encasements (An et al., 2006; Meyer et al., 2009; Nielsen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Exosomes accumulate to a high degree in both papillae and encasements.
source: The strong extracellular accumulation of GFP-PEN1 signal localized to fungal attack sites can be explained by the secretion of extracellular vesicles, also known as exosomes, which accumulate to a high degree in both papillae and encasements (An et al., 2006; Meyer et al., 2009; Nielsen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Exosomes are suggested to contain miRNAs directed against the invading pathogen.
source: While exosomes are suggested to contain miRNAs directed against the invading pathogen, their topology makes it difficult to associate syntaxin functionality (Meyer et al., 2009; Hansen and Nielsen, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: GFP-PEN1 is generally considered a valid exosomal marker.
source: GFP-PEN1 is generally considered a valid exosomal marker, yet the biogenesis pathway of PEN1-labeled exosomes remains unclear (Rutter and Innes, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents current scientific understanding.

claim: The biogenesis pathway of PEN1-labeled exosomes remains unclear.
source: GFP-PEN1 is generally considered a valid exosomal marker, yet the biogenesis pathway of PEN1-labeled exosomes remains unclear (Rutter and Innes, 2017).
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: Loss of PEN1 or ROR2 delays, but does not prevent, the papilla response upon attack by the barley powdery mildew fungus Bgh in Arabidopsis or barley, respectively.
source: Loss of PEN1 or ROR2 delays, but does not prevent, the papilla response upon attack by the barley powdery mildew fungus Bgh in Arabidopsis or barley, respectively (Assaad et al., 2004; Böhlenius et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The deposition of encasements around developing intracellular pathogenic structures (IPS) is unaffected by the loss of PEN1.
source: In contrast, the deposition of encasements around developing intracellular pathogenic structures (IPS) is unaffected by the loss of PEN1 (Wen et al., 2011; Nielsen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The PEN1- and ROR2-dependent immunity appears dedicated toward the haustorium-forming powdery mildew and rust fungi.
source: Furthermore, although many other filamentous pathogens also penetrate directly through the plant epidermal cell wall, the PEN1- and ROR2-dependent immunity appears dedicated toward the haustorium-forming powdery mildew and rust fungi (Collins et al., 2003; Jarosch et al., 2005; Lipka et al., 2005; Loehrer et al., 2008; Hoefle et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The molecular mechanisms underlying papilla/encasement formation, as well as their role in general plant pre- and postinvasive immunity toward other filamentous pathogens, remain obscure.
source: Thus, the molecular mechanisms underlying papilla/encasement formation, as well as their role in general plant pre- and postinvasive immunity toward other filamentous pathogens, remain obscure.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current scientific knowledge.

claim: PEN1 and ROR2 belong to the SYP12 clade of secretory syntaxins, which first appears in embryophytes and is conserved in all land plants.
source: PEN1 and ROR2 belong to the SYP12 clade of secretory syntaxins, which first appears in embryophytes and is conserved in all land plants (Slane et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The appearance of the SYP12 clade was proposed to play a key role in the terrestrialization of plants by enabling specialization of the secretory pathway.
source: Consequently, the appearance of the SYP12 clade was proposed to play a key role in the terrestrialization of plants by enabling specialization of the secretory pathway (Sanderfoot, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Four of the five SYP12 clade members in Arabidopsis function in specialized forms of polarized secretion.
source: This is supported by the fact that four of the five SYP12 clade members in Arabidopsis function in specialized forms of polarized secretion, these being preinvasive immunity toward powdery mildew fungi (PEN1), root hair tip growth (SYP123), and pollen tube tip growth (SYP124 and SYP125) (Collins et al., 2003; Slane et al., 2017; Ichikawa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PEN1 and SYP122 were suggested to mediate distinct but complementary secretory pathways during vegetative plant growth.
source: Recently, PEN1 and SYP122, which is the closest homologue of PEN1, were suggested to mediate distinct but complementary secretory pathways during vegetative plant growth (Waghmare et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: syp122 mutants show an altered cell wall composition.
source: Indeed, syp122 mutants show an altered cell wall composition, but in contrast to pen1 mutants, there is no effect on the preinvasive immunity toward Bgh (Assaad et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In contrast to pen1 mutants, syp122 mutants show no effect on the preinvasive immunity toward Bgh.
source: Indeed, syp122 mutants show an altered cell wall composition, but in contrast to pen1 mutants, there is no effect on the preinvasive immunity toward Bgh (Assaad et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The pen1 syp122 double mutant is autoimmune, developing a severe necrotic phenotype and accumulating the defense hormone salicylic acid.
source: Interestingly, the pen1 syp122 double mutant is autoimmune, developing a severe necrotic phenotype and accumulating the defense hormone salicylic acid (Assaad et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Prior to the onset of necrosis, pen1 syp122 double mutant plants are indistinguishable from wild-type plants.
source: However, prior to the onset of necrosis, pen1 syp122 double mutant plants are indistinguishable from wild-type plants.
evidence: This is an observation from previous research.

claim: PEN1 and SYP122 likely mediate a highly specialized form of secretion, whereas general secretion relies on the evolutionarily ancient Qa-SNARE SYP132.
source: This underlines that PEN1 and SYP122 likely mediate a highly specialized form of secretion, whereas general secretion relies on the evolutionarily ancient Qa-SNARE SYP132 (Park et al., 2018; Karnahl et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The development of necrotic lesions in pen1 syp122 double mutant plants is markedly delayed when the accumulation of salicylic acid is hampered.
source: The development of necrotic lesions in pen1 syp122 double mutant plants is markedly delayed when the accumulation of salicylic acid is hampered (Zhang et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The pen1 syp122 double mutant autoimmune phenotype was suggested to result from activation of nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat receptors (NLRs).
source: Accordingly, the pen1 syp122 double mutant autoimmune phenotype was suggested to result from activation of nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat receptors (NLRs), immune sensors that recognize pathogen effectors, directly or indirectly, which leads to a programmed cell death response (Wang et al., 2019a; Wang et al., 2019b; Horsefield et al., 2019; Wan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mutations in the deubiquitinase AMSH3 that impairs the cell death reaction caused by activation of coiled-coil (CC)-NLRs also suppress the autoimmune phenotype of the pen1 syp122 double mutant.
source: In support of this, mutations in the deubiquitinase AMSH3 that impairs the cell death reaction caused by activation of coiled-coil (CC)-NLRs also suppress the autoimmune phenotype of the pen1 syp122 double mutant (Schultz-Larsen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: PEN1 and SYP122 are likely to have separate functions in the preinvasive immunity toward Bgh.
source: The autoimmune phenotype shows that while PEN1 and SYP122 are likely to have separate functions in the preinvasive immunity toward Bgh, the two syntaxins also share an as-yet unresolved function that is likely related to defense and not general development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed phenotypes.

claim: PEN1 and SYP122 share an as-yet unresolved function that is likely related to defense and not general development.
source: The autoimmune phenotype shows that while PEN1 and SYP122 are likely to have separate functions in the preinvasive immunity toward Bgh, the two syntaxins also share an as-yet unresolved function that is likely related to defense and not general development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed phenotypes.

claim: The pen1 syp122 mutant developed spontaneous callose deposits despite having a wild-type-like appearance.
source: From analysis of unattacked plants, we found that the pen1 syp122 mutant developed spontaneous callose deposits despite having a wild-type-like appearance (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in the figure.

claim: Callose is a polysaccharide (β-1,3-glucan) secreted in response to various biotic and abiotic stresses and is a major constituent of papillae and encasements.
source: Callose is a polysaccharide (β-1,3-glucan) secreted in response to various biotic and abiotic stresses and is a major constituent of papillae and encasements.
evidence: This is established knowledge about callose.

claim: The deposition of callose is not required to block the penetration event by Bgh per se, but it serves as a reliable visual marker for easy detection of papillae and encasements.
source: Although the deposition of callose is not required to block the penetration event by Bgh per se, it serves as a reliable visual marker for easy detection of papillae and encasements (Ellinger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Plants lacking PEN1 and SYP122 were unable to form papillae at sites of unsuccessful attack by fungal appressoria, as visualized by detection of callose.
source: We found that in response to attack by Bgh plants lacking PEN1 and SYP122 were unable to form papillae at sites of unsuccessful attack by fungal appressoria, as visualized by detection of callose (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and visual evidence.

claim: In pen1 syp122 mutants, the appressorial germ tube did not induce a papilla response, but large callosic deposits were induced by the noninvasive primary germ tube.
source: Surprisingly, while the appressorial germ tube did not induce a papilla response in pen1 syp122 mutants, we observed large callosic deposits induced by the noninvasive primary germ tube, which were not observed in any other genetic background (Figure 1D, F, and G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in the figures.

claim: SYP122 plays a complementary role to PEN1 in papilla formation upon attack by Bgh.
source: Thus, SYP122 seems to play a complementary role to PEN1 in papilla formation upon attack by Bgh.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Despite being unable to form a papilla at the attempted entry site, the pen1 syp122 mutant remains capable of generating focused depositions of callose elsewhere.
source: However, despite being unable to form a papilla at the attempted entry site, the pen1 syp122 mutant remains capable of generating focused depositions of callose elsewhere and seems to be highly sensitive to signals released by Bgh.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The pen1 syp122 mutant seems to be highly sensitive to signals released by Bgh.
source: However, despite being unable to form a papilla at the attempted entry site, the pen1 syp122 mutant remains capable of generating focused depositions of callose elsewhere and seems to be highly sensitive to signals released by Bgh.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed callose deposition patterns.

claim: In response to a successful penetration attempt by Bgh, the host cell initiates postinvasive immunity, where an encasement forms as an extension of the penetrated papilla.
source: In response to a successful penetration attempt by Bgh, the host cell initiates postinvasive immunity, where an encasement forms as an extension of the penetrated papilla (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by visual evidence in the figure.

claim: The successful penetration of pen1 syp122 cells often induced a strong but diffuse, unfocused accumulation of callose at the fungal entry site.
source: In contrast to our observations of unsuccessful penetration sites, the successful penetration of pen1 syp122 cells often induced a strong but diffuse, unfocused accumulation of callose at the fungal entry site (Figure 1E–G, Figure 1—video 1, Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in the figures and videos.

claim: No encasement-like structures were observed in pen1 syp122 mutants in response to successful penetration by Bgh.
source: Interestingly, we did not observe any encasement-like structures.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The callosic deposits in the pen1 syp122 mutant were superficial and did not extend inward from the outer surface of the host cell enveloping the growing IPS.
source: Instead, the callosic deposits in the pen1 syp122 mutant were superficial and did not extend inward from the outer surface of the host cell enveloping the growing IPS.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The penetration event by Bgh triggers a strong callose response, but formation of the encasement is dependent on a functional overlap of the PEN1 and SYP122 syntaxins.
source: This would suggest that the penetration event by Bgh triggers a strong callose response, but formation of the encasement is dependent on a functional overlap of the PEN1 and SYP122 syntaxins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: IPS formation by G. orontii seemed unaffected in pen1 syp122 and no encasements were found.
source: For G. orontii, IPS formation seemed unaffected in pen1 syp122 and no encasements were found.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Successful penetration by G. orontii did not induce the strong, diffuse callose response described for Bgh in pen1 syp122 mutants.
source: Interestingly, successful penetration by G. orontii did not induce the strong, diffuse callose response described for Bgh (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D, Figure 1—video 3, Figure 1—video 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in the figures and videos.

claim: TET8-GFP (TETRASPANIN 8) accumulates at sites of attack by Botrytis.
source: We speculated that the plant exosomal marker TET8-GFP (TETRASPANIN 8), which accumulates at sites of attack by Botrytis, would also accumulate in response to attack by Bgh (Boavida et al., 2013; Cai et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In unattacked epidermal cells of wild-type plants, TET8-GFP localized mainly on the plasma membrane.
source: In unattacked epidermal cells of wild-type plants, we found TET8-GFP localized mainly on the plasma membrane (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in the figure.

claim: TET8-GFP signal focally accumulated in response to successful penetration by Bgh and seems a reliable marker for the encasement.
source: TET8-GFP signal focally accumulated in response to successful penetration by Bgh and seems a reliable marker for the encasement (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in the figure.

claim: In unattacked epidermal cells of the pen1 syp122 mutant, the TET8-GFP localization was similar to that seen in wild-type plants.
source: In unattacked epidermal cells of the pen1 syp122 mutant, the TET8-GFP localization was similar to that seen in wild-type plants, whereas successful penetration by Bgh did not induce focal accumulation of TET8-GFP (Figure 2C and D, Figure 2—video 1, Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in the figures and videos.

claim: Successful penetration by Bgh did not induce focal accumulation of TET8-GFP in pen1 syp122 mutants.
source: In unattacked epidermal cells of the pen1 syp122 mutant, the TET8-GFP localization was similar to that seen in wild-type plants, whereas successful penetration by Bgh did not induce focal accumulation of TET8-GFP (Figure 2C and D, Figure 2—video 1, Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in the figures and videos.

claim: The general localization of TET8-GFP was not affected in the pen1 syp122 mutant.
source: Thus, the general localization of TET8-GFP was not affected in the pen1 syp122 mutant.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: PEN1 and SYP122 play a specific role in pre- and postinvasive immunity.
source: Only in the event of fungal attack where TET8-GFP is transported to the infection site in wild-type plants this did not occur in the double mutant, supporting the idea that PEN1 and SYP122 play a specific role in pre- and postinvasive immunity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: The loss of FMO1 clearly relieves the downstream effects of the pen1 syp122 lesion-mimic mutant.
source: Similar to introducing a number of SA-signaling mutations, the loss of FMO1 clearly relieves the downstream effects of the pen1 syp122 lesion-mimic mutant (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in the figure.

claim: Mutations in SA-signaling do not affect preinvasive immunity toward Bgh.
source: However, importantly, these mutations do not affect preinvasive immunity toward Bgh, thereby clearly separating the two phenotypes mechanistically (Zhang et al., 2007 and this work).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research and data from this study.

claim: fmo1 pen1 syp122 plants did not display the large callosic deposits induced by the noninvasive primary germ tube.
source: Moreover, fmo1 pen1 syp122 plants did not display the large callosic deposits induced by the noninvasive primary germ tube.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: During the initial 48 hr after inoculation with G. orontii, formation of the IPS and secondary hyphae in fmo1 pen1 syp122 was indistinguishable from the fmo1 control plants.
source: During the initial 48 hr after inoculation, we found that formation of the IPS and secondary hyphae in fmo1 pen1 syp122 was indistinguishable from the fmo1 control plants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in the figure.

claim: fmo1 plants formed papillae at the site of attack by Bgh that were identical to wild-type as visualized by detection of callose.
source: In response to attack by Bgh, we found that fmo1 plants formed papillae at the site of attack that were identical to wild-type as visualized by detection of callose (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in the figures.

claim: Plants lacking PEN1 and SYP122 were unable to form discrete papillae at sites of unsuccessful fungal attack by Bgh.
source: Instead, plants lacking PEN1 and SYP122 were unable to form discrete papillae at sites of unsuccessful fungal attack.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: fmo1 pen1 syp122 plants failed to accumulate papillary H2O2 in response to attack by Bgh.
source: In accordance with our observations on callose deposition, we found that fmo1 pen1 syp122 plants failed to accumulate papillary H2O2 (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in the figure.

claim: Plants lacking PEN1 and SYP122 failed to form papillae at sites of attack by Bgh.
source: Thus, these results confirmed that plants lacking PEN1 and SYP122 failed to form papillae at sites of attack by Bgh.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data.

claim: fmo1 mutants reacted like wild-type plants in response to successful penetration by Bgh, as visualized by the detection of callose encasements around the IPS.
source: Similar to the papilla response, we found that fmo1 mutants reacted like wild-type plants in response to successful penetration by Bgh, as visualized by the detection of callose encasements around the IPS (Figure 4A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in the figures.

claim: fmo1 pen1 syp122 plants were unable to create an encasement around the developing IPS when penetrated by Bgh.
source: In stark contrast to this, fmo1 pen1 syp122 plants were unable to create an encasement around the developing IPS when penetrated by Bgh.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: In fmo1 pen1 syp122 plants, successful penetration by Bgh induced a diffuse, superficial accumulation of H2O2, but no encasement-like structures were observed.
source: We found that in fmo1 pen1 syp122 plants successful penetration by Bgh induced a diffuse, superficial accumulation of H2O2, but we did not observe encasement-like structures (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in the figure.

claim: Plants lacking PEN1 and SYP122 failed to form encasements at sites of attack by Bgh.
source: This supported our finding that plants lacking PEN1 and SYP122 failed to form encasements at sites of attack.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data.

claim: Fungal development and host cell responses in pad4 sid2 pen1 syp122 and amsh3 pen1 syp122 mutants were similar to that observed in fmo1 pen1 syp122 plants.
source: As expected, fungal development and host cell responses in these lines were similar to that observed in fmo1 pen1 syp122 plants (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Figure 4—videos 1–8).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in the figures and videos.

claim: There was a significant increase in fungal penetration frequency on fmo1 pen1 syp122 plants when compared to pen1 single and fmo1 pen1 double mutant plants.
source: We found a significant increase in fungal penetration frequency on fmo1 pen1 syp122 plants when compared to pen1 single and fmo1 pen1 double mutant plants (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in the figure.

claim: The Bgh-induced formation of papillae and encasements at attack sites is dependent on a functional overlap between the PEN1 and SYP122 syntaxins.
source: Taken together, these observations show that the Bgh-induced formation of papillae and encasements at attack sites is dependent on a functional overlap between the PEN1 and SYP122 syntaxins.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data.

claim: Preinvasive immunity toward C. destructivum in Arabidopsis does not require PEN1.
source: Nevertheless, while host cell responses include papilla formation, the highly effective preinvasive immunity of Arabidopsis toward nonadapted Colletotrichum species such as C. destructivum does not require PEN1 (Shimada et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Attack by C. destructivum did not induce accumulation of GFP-PEN1, GFP-SYP122, or TET8-GFP at sites of attempted penetration.
source: Moreover, attack by C. destructivum did not induce accumulation of GFP-PEN1, GFP-SYP122, or TET8-GFP at sites of attempted penetration (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in the figure.

claim: Plants lacking both PEN1 and SYP122 showed a dramatic decrease in the ability to form papillae at sites of unsuccessful penetration by C. destructivum.
source: Nonetheless, we found that plants lacking both PEN1 and SYP122 showed a dramatic decrease in the ability to form papillae at sites of unsuccessful penetration (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in the figure.

claim: The host cell response to penetration by C. destructivum only rarely resulted in the formation of a detectable encasement.
source: In contrast to Bgh, the host cell response to penetration by C. destructivum only rarely resulted in the formation of a detectable encasement.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: In fmo1 pen1 syp122, the responses to C. destructivum varied from no detectable callose to a faint diffuse accumulation of callose at the penetration site.

claim: fmo1 pen1 syp122 plants displayed elevated penetration frequencies when attacked by P. infestans.

claim: No increase in penetration events by P. infestans was detected in the syp123 mutant, even when in combination with pen1.

claim: PEN1 or SYP122 are required for papilla and encasement responses, which mediate immunity toward phylogenetically distant, nonadapted filamentous pathogens.
source: Taken together, these findings show that PEN1 or SYP122 are required for papilla and encasement responses, which mediate immunity toward these phylogenetically distant, nonadapted filamentous pathogens.

claim: The functionality of PEN1 and SYP122 in immunity does not correlate with the ability of these syntaxins to visibly accumulate at attack sites.
source: Moreover, it is striking that the functionality of PEN1 and SYP122 in immunity does not correlate with the ability of these syntaxins to visibly accumulate at attack sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: The germinating spores of Bgh were not able to properly differentiate a penetration hypha or appressorium on Marchantia thalli.

source: Similarly, most spores of P. infestans germinating on Marchantia seemed unable to identify a host cell and direct an attack.

claim: Occasional sites of attempted and successful penetrations by P. infestans were detected on Marchantia, to which the host cell responded by forming papillae and encasement-like defense structures, respectively.

claim: The cellular responses of Marchantia to C. destructivum were similar to those observed in Arabidopsis.
source: Thus, the cellular responses of Marchantia to C. destructivum were similar to those that we observed in Arabidopsis.

claim: GFP-MpSYP12B only partially suppressed the necrotic and dwarfed phenotypes of pen1 syp122 plants.
source: GFP-MpSYP12A fully suppressed the necrotic and dwarfed phenotypes of pen1 syp122 plants, while GFP-MpSYP12B only partially suppressed these phenotypes (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in the figure.

claim: Expression of either of the two SYP13 clade members, MpSYP13A and MpSYP13B, failed to rescue the pen1 syp122 mutant.
source: In contrast, expression of either of the two SYP13 clade members, MpSYP13A and MpSYP13B, failed to rescue the pen1 syp122 mutant.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: MpSYP12A shares the PEN1/SYP122 overlapping function.
source: This suggests that MpSYP12A shares the PEN1/SYP122 overlapping function and that MpSYP12B does so incompletely.

claim: MpSYP12B incompletely shares the PEN1/SYP122 overlapping function.
source: This suggests that MpSYP12A shares the PEN1/SYP122 overlapping function and that MpSYP12B does so incompletely.
evidence: This is an inference based on the complementation data.

source: In contrast, neither GFP-SYP122 nor the two GFP-MpSYP12s accumulated in papillae at sites of attempted penetration (Figure 8C, Figure 8—figure supplement 4).

claim: Preinvasive immunity toward Bgh was not restored by GFP-MpSYP12A.

claim: MpSYP12A resembles SYP122, and not PEN1, both in its localization and functionality.
source: Thus, MpSYP12A resembles SYP122, and not PEN1, both in its localization and functionality.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data.

claim: GFP-MpSYP12A fully restored immunity toward both P. infestans and C. destructivum.
source: In support of this, GFP-MpSYP12A fully restored immunity toward both P. infestans and C. destructivum (Figure 8F, Figure 8—figure supplement 6A and B).

source: Also, when tested with the adapted filamentous pathogens G. orontii and Colletotrichum higginsianum, penetration frequencies were similar to plants expressing PEN1 and SYP122 (Figure 8—figure supplement 6C and D).

claim: Focal accumulation of GFP-MpSYP12A or GFP-MpSYP12B was not observed at unsuccessful attack sites by either C. destructivum or P. infestans.
source: As described for PEN1 and SYP122, focal accumulation of GFP-MpSYP12A or GFP-MpSYP12B was not observed at unsuccessful attack sites by either C. destructivum or P. infestans (Figure 8—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and visual evidence in the figure.

claim: These results reveal a conserved SYP12 clade functionality that has survived 470 My of independent evolution.
source: Taken together, these results reveal a conserved SYP12 clade functionality that has survived 470 My of independent evolution.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data and evolutionary timescales.

claim: The PEN1-dependent immunity toward powdery mildew fungi evolved at a later stage of land plant evolution.
source: Moreover, our findings suggest that the PEN1-dependent immunity toward powdery mildew fungi evolved at a later stage of land plant evolution.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The pen1 syp122 mutant lacks papillae and encasements, but epidermal cells are still able to respond to pathogen-derived signals in a polarized fashion.
source: It is noteworthy that although the pen1 syp122 double mutant lacks these defense structures, epidermal cells are still able to respond to pathogen-derived signals in a polarized fashion, as seen in responses to the nonpenetrative primary germ tube of Bgh.

claim: Neither the general ability to secrete callose, generate H2O2, nor the underlying mechanism needed for polarized secretion are dependent on PEN1 and SYP122.
source: This underlines that neither the general ability to secrete callose, generate H2O2, nor the underlying mechanism needed for polarized secretion are dependent on PEN1 and SYP122.

source: Instead, we suggest that the PEN1/SYP122-dependent papillae and encasements are defense structures that enable a focused secretion, specifically aimed at blocking the ingress of filamentous pathogens.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Knockdown of StSYR1 in potato, a homolog of PEN1, results in reduced papilla formation in response to P. infestans.
source: In support of this, knockdown of StSYR1 in potato, a homolog of PEN1, results in reduced papilla formation in response to P. infestans (Eschen-Lippold et al., 2012).

claim: Loss of papillae/encasements correlates with the loss of general preinvasive immunity.
source: Instead, we have shown here that loss of papillae/encasements correlates with the loss of general preinvasive immunity.

claim: It is unlikely that accumulation of callose, H2O2, syntaxins, or even TET8 would have a direct effect on the pathogen.
source: Also, we find it unlikely that accumulation of callose, H2O2, syntaxins, or even TET8 would have a direct effect on the pathogen.

claim: Neither PEN1, SYP122, nor TET8 focally accumulate in response to attack by C. destructivum or P. infestans, despite the formation of papillae.
source: This is supported by our observations that neither PEN1, SYP122, nor TET8 focally accumulate in response to attack by C. destructivum or P. infestans, despite the formation of papillae.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Papillae and encasements serve as defense structures that contain a complex mixture of exosomes, toxic metabolites, and/or antimicrobial enzymes and peptides that mediate immunity.
source: Instead, our findings reinforce the idea that papillae and encasements serve as defense structures that contain a complex mixture of exosomes, toxic metabolites, and/or antimicrobial enzymes and peptides that mediate immunity (Kwon et al., 2008).

claim: Cargo molecules are likely delivered in a PEN1- and SYP122-dependent manner to the site of attack to form papillae/encasements and thus prevent pathogen ingress.
source: It is likely that these cargo molecules are delivered in a PEN1- and SYP122-dependent manner to the site of attack to form papillae/encasements and thus prevent pathogen ingress.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Preinvasive immunity correlates with the timely formation of papillae.
source: Previous studies on the interaction between Arabidopsis and Bgh have revealed that preinvasive immunity correlates with the timely formation of papillae.

claim: The fast papilla response likely requires the recycling of papilla material in a process involving PEN1 and GNOM.
source: This fast response likely requires the recycling of papilla material in a process involving PEN1 and GNOM (Nielsen et al., 2012).

claim: PEN1 and SYP122 mediate the secretion of distinct cargo subsets.
source: Previous studies have shown that PEN1 and SYP122 mediate the secretion of distinct cargo subsets, which may explain their differing contributions to preinvasive immunity (Waghmare et al., 2018).

claim: PEN1 and SYP122 functionally overlap in the formation of papillae and encasements.
source: Based on the work presented here, it is now evident that PEN1 and SYP122 functionally overlap in the formation of papillae and encasements.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data.

claim: PEN1 serves two functions in preinvasive immunity: one mediates a fast mobilization of papilla material, while the second function is shared with SYP122 and contributes to a more general papilla and encasement response to filamentous pathogens.
source: This could be explained by PEN1 serving two functions in preinvasive immunity. The first mediates a fast mobilization of papilla material, while the second function is shared with SYP122 and contributes to a more general papilla and encasement response to filamentous pathogens (Figure 9).

claim: The fast mobilization of papilla material is likely related to the ability of PEN1 to shuttle between the plasma membrane and trans-Golgi network, which is less prominent for SYP122.
source: The fast mobilization of papilla material is likely related to the ability of PEN1 to shuttle between the plasma membrane and trans-Golgi network, which is less prominent for SYP122 (Hansen and Nielsen, 2017; Nielsen and Thordal-Christensen, 2012; Nielsen and Thordal-Christensen, 2013).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PEN1, and less so SYP122, could function at the trans-Golgi network, receiving vesicles from the plasma membrane that mediate the fast GNOM-dependent recycling of papilla material.
source: Consequently, PEN1, and less so SYP122, could function at the trans-Golgi network, receiving vesicles from the plasma membrane that mediate the fast GNOM-dependent recycling of papilla material, warding off the powdery mildew fungus.

claim: The differences in papilla content based on observations of GFP-PEN1, GFP-SYP122, and TET8-GFP result from the involvement of distinct pathways for delivering cargo vesicles to the papilla.
source: Therefore, we speculate that the differences in papilla content based on observations of GFP-PEN1, GFP-SYP122, and TET8-GFP result from the involvement of distinct pathways for delivering cargo vesicles to the papilla.

claim: The host cell might be able to differentiate the response according to the attacker.
source: Alternatively, as the accumulation of some papilla cargos is triggered by only a subset of pathogens, the host cell might be able to differentiate the response according to the attacker.

claim: These pathways share a common requirement for PEN1 or SYP122 to mediate vesicle fusion with the plasma membrane at pathogen attack sites.
source: Nonetheless, these pathways share a common requirement for PEN1 or SYP122 to mediate vesicle fusion with the plasma membrane at pathogen attack sites.

claim: Preinvasive immunity toward filamentous pathogens could also involve other molecular pathways that act independently of PEN1 and SYP122.
source: In addition, because some spores fail to penetrate, even in the complete absence of papillae and encasements, preinvasive immunity toward filamentous pathogens could also involve other molecular pathways that act independently of PEN1 and SYP122.

source: In this regard, preinvasive immunity mediated by PEN2 and PEN3, as well as the resistance gained by loss of MLO, is of particular interest since both pathways seem to function independently of PEN1 (Lipka et al., 2005; Stein et al., 2006; Kuhn et al., 2017).

source: It remains to be elucidated if these preinvasive immunity pathways also function independently of SYP122.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge.

source: The SYP12 clade of plant secretory syntaxins is thought to have evolved during colonization of the land and is conserved in all land plants so far examined (Slane et al., 2017).

source: Because terrestrialization presented enormous challenges to plants, the SYP12 clade was suggested to have acquired specialized roles in secretion needed to facilitate this transition (Sanderfoot, 2007).

claim: Powdery mildews, root hairs, and pollen tubes did not exist until long after the onset of plant terrestrialization.
source: However, powdery mildews, root hairs, and pollen tubes did not exist until long after the onset of plant terrestrialization.

source: Also, the interaction motifs needed for Kv channel interaction are restricted to vascular plants (Karnik et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

source: Our discovery that SYP12A from Marchantia can complement SYP122, but not PEN1, in Arabidopsis reveals a conserved syntaxin functionality spanning 470 My of independent evolution.

claim: The functionality of the original SYP12 clade syntaxins is likely to have been similar to that of MpSYP12A and SYP122.
source: Therefore, the functionality of the original SYP12 clade syntaxins is likely to have been similar to that of MpSYP12A and SYP122.

source: Interestingly, in Marchantia, MpSYP12A locates to the plasma membrane and seems vital for cell plate formation, whereas MpSYP12B locates to a type of oil body unique to liverworts (Kanazawa et al., 2016; Kanazawa et al., 2020).

source: Interestingly, in Marchantia, MpSYP12A locates to the plasma membrane and seems vital for cell plate formation, whereas MpSYP12B locates to a type of oil body unique to liverworts (Kanazawa et al., 2016; Kanazawa et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

source: We suggest that MpSYP12A and SYP122 represent the original SYP12 clade functionality in land plants, which provides a highly conserved and effective broad-spectrum immunity toward filamentous pathogens.

source: Before plant terrestrialization, the land was already colonized by filamentous fungi that were able to degrade cell walls and to utilize living or dead plant tissue as a nutrient source (Chang et al., 2015).

source: These mutualistic interactions are thought to have resulted from ancestral land plants being able to 'tame' early saprophytic filamentous fungi (Chang et al., 2015; Berbee et al., 2017).

source: We envisage that the SYP12 syntaxins enabled early land plants to regulate fungal entry and colonization, and that over time this leads to the mutually beneficial interactions that facilitated terrestrialization.

source: Our finding that plants could rely on a common membrane trafficking pathway to block pathogen entry should lead to new insights into how successful pathogens defeat this immunity by means of effector proteins (Jones et al., 2016).
